latin: UBI HAROLD DUX ANGLORUM ET SUI MILITES EQUITANT AD BOSHAM ECCLESIA
english: Where Harold, Duke of the English, and his knights ride to Bosham Church
context: The tapestry begins in 1064. King Edward the Confessor sends Harold Godwinson on a diplomatic mission to Normandy. Harold rides to his coastal estate at Bosham and prays at the local church before setting sail.

latin: HIC HAROLD MARE NAVIGAVIT
english: Here Harold sailed by sea
context: Harold and his men board their ships with hunting dogs and falcons. These animals signal that this is a peaceful diplomatic mission, not a military expedition.

latin: ET VELIS VENTO PLENIS VENIT IN TERRAM WIDONIS COMITIS
english: and with sails filled with wind came to the land of Count Wido
context: A storm blows Harold's fleet off course across the English Channel. They land in Ponthieu, where Count Guy (Wido) immediately seizes Harold in hopes of demanding a massive ransom.

latin: HIC APPREHENDIT WIDO HAROLDU
english: Here Wido seized Harold
context: Guy (Wido) of Ponthieu captures Harold. Shipwrecked travelers were often held for ransom in the Middle Ages. Harold is taken prisoner.

latin: ET DUXIT EUM AD BELREM ET IBI EUM TENUIT
english: and led him to Beaurain and held him there
context: Harold is taken to Guy's stronghold at Beaurain. He is treated as a high-value prisoner rather than a common captive.

latin: UBI HAROLD ET WIDO PARABOLANT
english: Where Harold and Wido converse
context: Guy and Harold converse. Guy is likely demanding a ransom or setting terms for Harold's captivity.

latin: UBI NUNTII WILLELMI DUCIS VENERUNT AD WIDONU
english: Where the messengers of Duke William came to Wido
context: Duke William of Normandy hears of Harold's capture and sends messengers to Guy of Ponthieu. William demands that Guy hand Harold over to him, as Guy is William's vassal.

latin: NUNTII WILLELMI
english: The messengers of William
context: The messengers arrive. Note the aggressive posture and the dwarf holding the horses, often identified as Turold.

latin: HIC VENIT NUNTIUS AD WILGELMUM DUCEM
english: Here the messenger came to Duke William
context: A messenger returns to William to report on the situation with Count Guy.

latin: HIC WIDO ADDUXIT HAROLDUM AD WILGELMUM NORMANNORUM DUCEM
english: Here Wido brought Harold to William, Duke of the Normans
context: Guy complies with William's demands and hands Harold over. This shifts Harold from being Guy's prisoner to William's 'guest' (and political pawn).

latin: HIC DUX WILGELM CUM HAROLDO VENIT AD PALATIUM SUUM
english: Here Duke William came to his palace with Harold
context: William takes Harold back to his palace at Rouen. This begins Harold's time accompanying William on campaigns in Normandy.

latin: UBI UNUS CLERICUS ET AELFGYVA
english: Where a certain cleric and Aelfgyva
context: This is one of the most mysterious scenes in the tapestry. Aelfgyva is an English name, and a cleric is touching her face or striking her. Its exact meaning has been lost to history, but it likely refers to a scandal familiar to contemporary audiences.

latin: HIC WILLELM DUX ET EXERCITUS EIUS VENERUNT AD MONTEM MICHAELIS
english: Here Duke William and his army came to Mont Saint-Michel
context: William and Harold go on a military campaign against Conan II, Duke of Brittany. They pass Mont Saint-Michel, a famous abbey on a tidal island.

latin: ET HIC TRANSIERUNT FLUMEN COSNONIS
english: and here they crossed the river Couesnon
context: The army crosses the river Couesnon, the border between Normandy and Brittany. The shifting sands of the river mouth were incredibly dangerous.

latin: HIC HAROLD DUX TRAHEBAT EOS DE ARENA
english: Here Duke Harold pulled them from the sand
context: Several Norman soldiers sink into the quicksand. Harold, shown displaying great physical strength, rescues two Norman soldiers from drowning.

latin: ET VENERUNT AD DOL ET CONAN FUGA VERTIT
english: and they came to Dol and Conan fled
context: The army arrives at Dol, forcing Conan to flee down a rope from his castle.

latin: HIC MILITES WILLELMI DUCIS PUGNANT CONTRA DINANTES
english: Here the knights of Duke William fight against the men of Dinan
context: The Norman army lays siege to the town of Dinan, fighting the Bretons.

latin: ET CUNAN CLAVES PORREXIT
english: and Conan surrendered the keys
context: Conan II surrenders Dinan to William, passing the keys to the castle on the tip of a lance.

latin: HIC WILLELM DEDIT ARMA HAROLDO
english: Here William gave arms to Harold
context: William rewards Harold for his bravery in the campaign by giving him arms (knighting him). This cements a feudal bond where Harold becomes William's subordinate in the Norman tradition.

latin: HIE
english: Here William came to Bayeux
context: The army arrives in Bayeux, the seat of Bishop Odo (William's half-brother), who likely commissioned this tapestry.

latin: UBI HAROLD SACRAMENTUM FECIT WILLELMO DUCI
english: Where Harold made an oath to Duke William
context: The climax of the Norman narrative: Harold swears a sacred oath on holy relics to support William's claim to the English throne. By later breaking this oath, Harold is cast as a perjurer, justifying William's invasion.

latin: HIC HAROLD DUX REVERSUS EST AD ANGLICAM TERRAM
english: Here Duke Harold returned to English land
context: Harold is released and sails back to England.

latin: ET VENIT AD EDWARDU REGEM
english: and he came to King Edward
context: Harold reports back to King Edward the Confessor. Edward appears frail and aged, foreshadowing his impending death.

latin: HIC PORTATUR CORPUS EADWARDI REGIS AD ECCLESIAM SCI PETRI APLI
english: Here the body of King Edward is carried to the Church of Saint Peter the Apostle
context: King Edward dies. The tapestry uses non-linear storytelling here: his body is carried to Westminster Abbey, the great church he just finished building, before his death bed scene is shown.

latin: HIC EADWARDUS REX IN LECTO ALLOQUIT FIDELES
english: Here King Edward in bed speaks to his faithful followers
context: On his deathbed, Edward speaks to his followers. English tradition claims he appointed Harold as his successor with his dying breath, complicating William's claim.

latin: ET HIC DEFUNCTUS EST
english: and here he died
context: Edward passes away on January 5, 1066.

latin: HIC DEDERUNT HAROLDO CORONA REGIS
english: Here they gave the king's crown to Harold
context: The English nobles offer the crown to Harold. He accepts, breaking the oath he made to William in Bayeux.

latin: HIC RESIDET HAROLD REX ANGLORUM
english: Here sits Harold King of the English
context: Harold is crowned King of England. He is shown holding the orb and sceptre, symbols of royal authority, with Archbishop Stigand nearby.

latin: ISTI MIRANT STELLA
english: These people marvel at the star
context: Halley's Comet appears in the sky in April 1066. The Anglo-Saxons view it as a terrible omen of doom, pointing at the comet in fear while a spectral invasion fleet is hinted at below.

latin: HIC NAVIS ANGLICA VENIT IN TERRAM WILLELMI DUCIS
english: Here an English ship came to the land of Duke William
context: News of Harold's coronation and the breaking of the oath reaches Duke William in Normandy. An English ship arrives with the message.

latin: HIC WILLELM DUX JUSSIT NAVES EDIFICARE
english: Here Duke William ordered ships to be built
context: William decides to invade England to claim the throne. He orders a massive fleet of transport ships to be built.

latin: HIC TRAHUNT NAVES AD MARE
english: Here they drag the ships to the sea
context: The Normans cut down trees and construct ships, dragging them to the sea in preparation for the invasion.

latin: ISTI PORTANT ARMAS AD NAVES ET HIC TRAHUNT CARRUM CUM VINO ET ARMIS
english: These men carry arms to the ships and here they drag a cart (laden) with wine and arms
context: Weapons, armor, and supplies (including large casks of wine) are loaded onto the ships.

latin: † HIC WILLELM DUX IN MAGNO NAVIGIO MARE TRANSIVIT ET VENIT AD PEVENESÆ
english: † Here Duke William in a great ship crossed the sea and came to Pevensey
context: The Norman fleet crosses the English Channel. William's flagship, the Mora, was a gift from his wife Matilda. They land at Pevensey in Sussex on September 28, 1066.

latin: HIC EXEUNT CABALLI DE NAVIBUS
english: Here the horses leave the ships
context: The valuable warhorses are unloaded from the ships. The Norman use of cavalry would prove decisive in the coming battle.

latin: ET HIC MILITES FESTINAVERUNT HESTINGA UT CIBUM RAPERENTUR
english: and here the knights have hurried to Hastings to seize food
context: The Norman army moves to Hastings and begins foraging for supplies, which involved pillaging the local English countryside to provoke Harold into battle.

latin: HIC COQUITUR CARO ET HIC MINISTRAVERUNT MINISTRI
english: Here the meat is being cooked and here the servants have served (it)
context: A feast is prepared. Meat is boiled and roasted on spits. This highlights the logistics of feeding a medieval army on campaign.

latin: HIC FECERUN PRANDIUM
english: Here they have a meal
context: Bishop Odo blesses the food at a banquet. The semicircular table resembles depictions of the Last Supper.

latin: ISTE JUSSIT UT FODERETUR CASTELLUM AT HESTENGA
english: He ordered that a motte should be dug at Hastings
context: William orders the construction of a motte-and-bailey castle at Hastings to secure his beachhead and protect his forces.

latin: HIC NUNTIATUM EST WILLELM DE HAROLD
english: Here William was told about Harold
context: A messenger informs William that Harold's army is approaching. Harold had just defeated a Norwegian invasion in the north and marched his army rapidly south to meet William.

latin: HIC DOMUS INCENDITUR
english: Here a house is burned
context: The Normans burn a local house, terrorizing the population. A woman and child flee the burning building.

latin: HIC MILITES EXIERUNT DE HESTENGA ET VENERUNT AD PRELIUM CONTRA HAROLDUM REGE
english: Here the knights have left Hastings and have come to the battle against King Harold
context: The Norman cavalry rides out from Hastings on the morning of October 14, 1066, to meet the English army in battle.

latin: HIC WILLELM DUX INTERROGAT VITAL SI VIDISSET HAROLDI EXERCITU
english: Here Duke William asks Vital if he has seen Harold's army
context: William asks his scout, Vital, if he has spotted Harold's forces.

latin: ISTE NUNTIAT HAROLDUM REGE DE EXERCITU WILLELMI DUCIS
english: This messenger tells King Harold about Duke William's army
context: An English scout spots the Norman army and reports back to King Harold.

latin: HIC WILLELM DUX ALLOQUITUR SUIS MILITIBUS UT PREPARAREN SE VIRILITER ET SAPIENTER AD PRELIUM CONTRA ANGLORUM EXERCITU
english: Here Duke William speaks to his knights to prepare themselves manfully and wisely for the battle against the army of the English
context: Duke William delivers a pre-battle speech to rally his troops, urging them to fight bravely.

latin: HIC CECIDERUNT LEWINE ET GYRÐ FRATRES HAROLDI REGIS
english: Here fell Leofwine and Gyrth , brothers of King Harold
context: The Battle of Hastings begins. The English form a shield wall on Senlac Hill. Harold's brothers, Leofwine and Gyrth, are killed early in the brutal fighting.

latin: HIC CECIDERUNT SIMUL ANGLI ET FRANCI IN PRELIO
english: Here English and French fell at the same time in battle
context: The fighting is fierce, with heavy casualties on both sides. Horses tumble, and the lower border is filled with the bodies of the dead and dying.

latin: HIC ODO EPS BACULU TENENS CONFORTAT PUEROS
english: Here Bishop Odo, holding a club, gives strength to the boys
context: A rumor spreads that William has been killed, causing the Normans to panic. Bishop Odo rides into the fray wielding a club to rally the fleeing troops.

latin: HIC EST WILLEL DUX
english: Here is Duke William
context: Duke William lifts his helmet to show his face to his men, proving he is still alive and restoring their morale.

latin: HIC HAROLD REX INTERFECTUS EST
english: Here King Harold was slain
context: The death of King Harold. He is traditionally identified as the figure with an arrow in his eye, though he may also be the figure being struck down by a Norman knight's sword. His death breaks the English resistance.

latin: ET FUGA VERTERUNT ANGLI
english: and the English have turned in flight
context: With their king dead, the English army collapses and flees the battlefield. The Normans are victorious, and William will become the Conqueror.
